source.reasoning_observation: At the same voltage, scaling wire length by 2 and diameter by 2 scales resistance by 1/2. Thus ideal power doubles. Matched initial/final water states require equal thermal energy, so heating time halves. No phase conversion is implied by a specified temperature rise.

target.decisive_route: An ideal model has input 90 W and loss 15 W, target energy 9000 J. A replacement model has resistance 3/4 of original at voltage 2/3 of original. Determine whether target can be reached and compare times. Shortest valid route: P₂/P₁=(2/3)²/(3/4)=16/27; P₂=160/3 W; net=115/3 W; t₂=5400/23 s≈234.78 s; t₁=120 s. Both positive. Check net power times time equals 9000 J.

core1a.scientific_construction: The input to a thermal system is energy per time. If an ideal resistor has resistance R=ρL/A, at fixed potential difference V its electrical input is V²/R. For a circular uniform wire A=πD²/4, so comparing otherwise identical material wires gives R₂/R₁=(L₂/L₁)/(D₂/D₁)². At fixed current instead, P=I²R. The circuit constraint changes the scaling. In an unchanged-phase system with a prescribed energy requirement E and a constant outward loss P_loss, the useful rate is P_in−P_loss. For positive useful power, t=E/(P_in−P_loss). These equations are supplied here as cross-topic model relations; this is not a practical heater-construction or mains-wiring exercise. A constant loss is an idealization, not a general heating law. A common endpoint requires matched mass, initial temperature and final state. At nonpositive net power the stipulated endpoint cannot be reached by positive accumulation.

worked_anchor.task: A hypothetical thermal simulator requires 18 kJ to reach its target. Its ideal input is 120 W and loss 20 W. A second simulated resistor has twice the length and twice the area of the first, supplied at the same voltage. Compare useful power and time.
worked_anchor.reasoning: Resistance unchanged because L/A unchanged; both have 120 W input, 100 W useful, and 180 s heating time. Confirm by 100×180=18000 J.

core1a.model_limits: Hypothetical model only; matched energy endpoints, positive net power, constant stated parameters and no unaccounted phase conversion.

core1b.task: A hypothetical heater model has input 180 W at fixed voltage, and the thermal system loses 30 W. Target internal-energy rise is 36000 J. A second model uses the same material, length 3/2 of the first and diameter twice the first, but the voltage is reduced to 3/4 of its original value. With the same constant loss, find resistance ratio, input and useful powers, and time ratio; verify the energy budget.

stages.predict: Predict whether the reduced voltage necessarily makes the second heating process slower.
stages.attempt: A hypothetical heater model has input 180 W at fixed voltage, and the thermal system loses 30 W. Target internal-energy rise is 36000 J. stages.reconstruct: R₂/R₁=(3/2)/4=3/8. P₂/P₁=(3/4)²/(3/8)=3/2; P₂=270 W, useful240 W. Original useful150 W, times240 s and150 s, ratio5/8. Both budgets give36000 J.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether you scaled diameter as area, used a fixed-current formula for fixed voltage, or omitted loss from the energy budget.
stages.repair: Write separate geometry, electrical input and thermal net-power ratios. Recompute the endpoint energy check.
stages.boundary_test: If instead input power were controlled to remain 180 W, would the geometry change alone alter heating time in this model?

core1b.boundary_response_criterion: No. Same input and loss imply same 150 W useful power and 240 s.
